# On Wandering Without a Map

I want to write about the strange experience of not knowing where to begin, which is itself a kind of beginning. There's something paradoxical about being asked to write freely—the freedom itself becomes a small weight, a blank field that asks to be filled with something other than its own emptiness. So perhaps the only honest way to start is by acknowledging that, and then walking forward anyway, the way you might step into a fog not because you can see the path but because standing still accomplishes even less.

I find myself thinking about attention, and how strange it is that this resource—so thin, so easily fractured—is the substance out of which everything we call a life gets made. Not time exactly, though time is the container. It's attention that does the work. Two people can live through the same hour and have entirely different relationships to it, depending on where their attention pooled and where it merely skimmed. I think about this when I try to remember a particular day from years ago and find that what I retained wasn't the event everyone else would call significant, but some small textural detail—light falling a certain way across a wall, the sound of a particular voice saying something inconsequential. The mind keeps its own ledger, and it rarely matches the official record.

There's a kind of humility in admitting that you don't control what you remember. We like to think of memory as something we curate, the way we curate a photo album, selecting the best images and discarding the blurry ones. But memory doesn't really work like that. It's less an album and more a series of accidents, sedimented over time, with certain moments calcifying into permanence for reasons that have nothing to do with their importance. The brain is not a reliable narrator of its own history. It tells the story it can tell, with the materials it happened to keep, and we mistake this haphazard archive for truth because it's the only archive we have.

I keep returning to this idea of accident, of contingency, because it seems to undercut so much of how we're taught to think about our lives. We're encouraged to believe in trajectories—that things lead to other things, that there's a logic unspooling beneath the surface of events, even if we can't always see it while we're living through it. And maybe there is such a logic, in retrospect, the way a river's path looks inevitable once it's carved its canyon. But in the moment, walking through your own days, there's so much more noise than signal. So many decisions made for reasons that seem important at the time and turn out to be irrelevant, and so many irrelevant-seeming moments that turn out, decades later, to have been hinges.

This is maybe why I'm suspicious of narratives that are too clean. The autobiography that reads like a novel, with foreshadowing and thematic unity—I understand the appeal, but I don't quite trust it. Lives don't have editors. They have entropy, mostly, punctuated by brief periods where things cohere, and then more entropy. The cohering periods are what we remember and what we tell stories about, but they're not necessarily representative of the whole. Most of life is the unremarkable connective tissue between the moments that feel like they mean something. And maybe that connective tissue is actually where most of living happens, even though it resists narrative.

I think about boredom in this context, and how we've come to treat it as a problem to be solved rather than a state to be inhabited. There's a way in which constant stimulation has eroded our capacity to sit inside an empty moment without flinching away from it. I notice this in myself—the reflexive reach for a device the second a queue gets long or a meeting goes quiet. It's not that I'm desperate for information in those moments. It's that the emptiness itself has become uncomfortable, almost unbearable, in a way it probably wasn't for people a few generations back, who had far fewer ways to escape their own unoccupied minds.

But I wonder if something gets lost in that escape. Boredom used to be, maybe still could be, a kind of fertile ground. Ideas that arrive unbidden often arrive in those gaps—in the shower, on a walk, in the strange liminal space between sleep and waking. These are the moments when the mind, not being actively managed, starts to make connections on its own, the way a fire left untended will sometimes find more interesting fuel than the fire you were carefully building. If we eliminate all the unmanaged moments, we might be eliminating the very conditions under which certain kinds of thought become possible.

This isn't a call to abandon technology or to romanticize some imagined simpler past—those arguments tend to flatten history into a morality play, and I don't think that's accurate or useful. People in every era have had their attention captured by something, whether it was gossip or religious obligation or the sheer effort of survival. The texture of distraction has changed, but the underlying tension—between the demands of the world and the needs of an interior life—seems to be a constant. What's different now is the deliberateness of the capture, the fact that entire industries are organized around the project of holding attention as long as possible, with techniques refined by extraordinary amounts of money and talent. That does seem like a meaningfully new condition, even if the basic struggle is old.

I keep thinking about the word "free" in "write freely," and how freedom, when you actually try to exercise it, often reveals itself to be constrained in ways you didn't notice until you tried to move. This is true of writing, certainly. You sit down to write whatever you want, and you discover almost immediately how much of what you "want" has been shaped by what you've read, what you think is expected, what genres and registers you have access to. True freedom, if it exists, might require a kind of unlearning that's almost impossible to do deliberately—you can't simply decide to forget the conventions you've absorbed. They're load-bearing walls in the structure of your thought, and pulling them out isn't a matter of will.

Maybe this is fine. Maybe the romantic idea of total freedom, total originality, was always a bit of a myth, and what's actually available to us is something more modest: the freedom to recombine what we've absorbed in slightly new configurations, to bring a particular sensibility to bear on inherited material. That's not nothing. Most of what we call originality, looked at closely, turns out to be recombination anyway. The artists we consider most singular were usually deeply, even obsessively, engaged with their predecessors. The originality was in the angle of approach, not in some impossible leap outside of influence altogether.

I think about how much of thinking is actually just noticing—paying attention to something that was already there, but unattended to. This seems undervalued as a creative act. We tend to valorize invention, the creation of something from nothing, but a huge amount of what feels like insight is really just attention finally landing on something it had been skating past. The object doesn't change. What changes is the quality of looking. And this suggests that one path toward having more interesting thoughts isn't necessarily to acquire more information, but to look more carefully at what's already available, to slow down the skating long enough for the landing to happen.

This is hard to do, though, because looking carefully takes time, and time is the resource that feels most scarce, even though, objectively, many of us have more discretionary time than most humans throughout history. The scarcity is partly manufactured—by the pace of work, the expectation of availability, the way leisure itself has become something to optimize rather than simply inhabit. But it's also partly real. There is something about the structure of contemporary life that fragments time into smaller and smaller units, so that even when you have an hour free, it doesn't feel like an hour—it feels like six overlapping ten-minute increments, each haunted by the awareness of what's coming next.

I wonder whether this fragmentation is part of why sustained attention feels increasingly rare and increasingly valuable. There's a kind of attention that can only happen across a longer arc—the attention required to read a long book, or to follow a complex argument across hundreds of pages, or to sit with a piece of music that unfolds slowly rather than hooking you in the first ten seconds. These longer forms require a kind of patience that the fragmented mode of contemporary attention doesn't cultivate. And I notice in myself a kind of muscle atrophy around this—a restlessness that sets in faster than it used to, an impulse to check whether something more interesting is happening elsewhere, even when what's in front of me is, by any reasonable measure, quite interesting.

Maybe this is just what it feels like to be a person living through a particular technological moment, and every era has its version of this complaint. I try to hold that perspective lightly—the awareness that complaints about modernity eroding attention or virtue or whatever else are about as old as writing itself. Socrates apparently worried that writing would weaken memory. People worried about the novel rotting minds, about television, about every subsequent medium. So there's a reasonable chance that this particular worry, about fragmented attention, will look quaint in retrospect, or will turn out to have been solved by some adaptation we can't yet see.

But even granting that historical pattern, I don't think it fully dissolves the concern. Each technology does change something real, even if humans adapt and even if the change isn't simply degradation. Maybe writing did change memory—made certain kinds of oral memorization unnecessary, while enabling other kinds of thought that weren't previously possible. The change isn't always bad, but it's still a change, and noticing the shape of the change seems worthwhile, even if we can't fully evaluate it from inside the moment of transition.

I want to step back from this thread, though, because I notice it's become a familiar groove—the meditation on attention and technology is a genre at this point, and I'm aware of slipping into its grooves rather than thinking freshly. So let me try to wander somewhere else.

I think about the strange comfort of routines, and how they function almost like a second skeleton, holding up a life that would otherwise feel formless. There's a particular pleasure in repetition that isn't about novelty at all—the pleasure of making the same coffee in the same way, of walking a familiar route and noticing the same landmarks. This kind of repetition isn't boring in the way that empty time can be boring; it's almost the opposite, a kind of groove that the mind can rest in without effort, freeing up attention for other things, or for nothing in particular, which might be its own kind of freedom.

I think rituals, even small mundane ones, work partly because they create a sense of continuity, a thread that runs through days that might otherwise feel disconnected from each other. Without that thread, time can start to feel like a series of disconnected rooms rather than a hallway. The ritual doesn't have to be meaningful in any grand sense—it just has to be reliable, a small anchor that makes the passage from one day to the next feel less like falling.

I notice that I'm drawn to write about process rather than content—about how thinking happens, how attention moves, how memory works—rather than landing on some particular subject and exploring it in depth. Maybe that's a kind of evasion, a way of staying abstract rather than risking something more specific and therefore more exposed. There's a vulnerability in writing about a particular memory, a particular person, a particular conviction, that's avoided by staying at this altitude, circling ideas about thought rather than thinking any one thought all the way through.

But maybe that's fine too. Not every piece of writing needs to plunge to the bottom of something. Some writing can just be a record of motion, a transcript of a mind moving across a stretch of time, touching down here and there without needing to settle. This is, after all, what was asked for—not an argument, not a story with a destination, just freedom, exercised for its own sake, for however long it takes to fill the space allotted.

I think there's something valuable in this kind of writing precisely because it's low-stakes in a particular way. There's no thesis to defend, no narrative arc that needs resolution. It's closer to the texture of actual thought, which rarely moves in straight lines, which doubles back and contradicts itself and changes the subject without warning. Most formal writing irons out this texture, replacing the actual mess of thinking with something more presentable. There's a kind of honesty in letting the mess show a little, even if it makes for a less satisfying read in conventional terms.

I notice the word count climbing toward some implicit endpoint, and I feel the pull to wrap things up, to find some way of bringing this back around to where it started, the way essays are taught to do—the circle that closes, the final line that echoes the first. But I'm not sure that impulse serves what I've actually been doing here, which is closer to wandering than to architecture. Maybe the more honest ending is just to stop, the way a walk ends not because you've arrived anywhere in particular, but because you've gone far enough, and turning back, or simply stopping, becomes the natural next thing.

So I'll stop here, with no particular conclusion, no thesis vindicated, just the record of an hour's attention moving across a handful of ideas—memory, boredom, freedom, repetition—touching each one lightly before moving to the next, the way you might walk through a house you've lived in for years, noticing things you usually don't bother to notice, simply because, for once, you had nowhere else you needed to be.
